1:
That the psalm is not new is the first thing they all say. Calvin calls it merely a part of the fortieth, and thinks the inscription may indicate as much, David having taken these five verses out of that psalm and accommodated them to some particular occasion; he will therefore only repeat the text, referring the reader elsewhere for interpretation. Clarke says it is almost word for word the last five verses of that psalm. Keil and Delitzsch place it after the sixty-ninth for the kindred nature of its contents, and describe what was done to it: the portion was detached and converted into the Elohimic style, so that David is plainly not the author in this stunted form, though the ascription holds if he composed the original here modified for liturgical use. Spurgeon calls it the second psalm that repeats another, the fifty-third having been a rehearsal of the fourteenth.

Where it differs from its original they mark closely. Keil and Delitzsch see the fragment betrayed at the first word, in the omission of the verb be pleased, so that the clause to deliver me, formerly governed by it, now belongs to make haste — and they suspect it may only accidentally have come to an independent existence. Spurgeon hears the same change as urgency: the fortieth begins be pleased, this begins make haste, or, as the Hebrew has it, with an abrupt and broken cry — O God, to deliver me; O Lord, to help me hasten. It is not forbidden us, he adds, in hours of dire distress, to ask for speed on God's part. The other difference, Elohim where the fortieth has Jehovah, he leaves unexplained: why it is done we know not, and the guesses of the critics may be right or not. Gill notes the same gap, that make haste has to be supplied from the clause following, and rejects the Targum reading, to deliver us.

The title puzzles them. Clarke finds little sense in it, and takes it to intimate that the psalm was a memorial that David had been in sore affliction and God had delivered him, as the Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic and Arabic understood it. Henry reads bringing to remembrance as putting God in mind of his mercy and promises — which is what we do when we plead with him, not that the Eternal Mind needs a remembrancer, but that this is an honour he puts upon the prayer of faith. Or rather it is to remind ourselves and others of former afflictions, that we may never be secure but always expect trouble, and of former devotions, that when the clouds return after the rain we may have recourse to the means we once found effectual.

Whether a man may pray twice in the same words Henry settles from the repetition itself. We may use in prayer the words we have often used before, since our Saviour in his agony prayed thrice, saying the same words; and David uses words he had used before, yet with some alterations, to show he did not mean to tie himself or others to them as a form — for God looks at the heart, not the words. Spurgeon draws the same lesson from having the psalm twice: as we have the words twice in the letter, let them be doubly with us in spirit, our frailty and many dangers making it a perpetual necessity to cry daily for deliverance. Clarke keeps to the plain distress: haste to help me, or I am lost. Augustine hears the voice of men troubled, and so of the Martyrs amid their sufferings, yet relying on their own Head: many members under one Head, bound in the bond of love and peace, are one man, and of that one man the voice is often heard in the Psalms, so that one cries as though it were all.
2:
The differences from the fortieth psalm are what the notes here mostly record. Ellicott counts two omissions in the first of these verses, the words together and to destroy it; Gill notes the same loss of together, and observes that where the fortieth had let them be desolate — which seems to respect their land and houses — this has a phrase that falls on their persons instead. On the next clause Ellicott suspects the copyist rather than the editor: where the fortieth reads and put to shame, this reads for a reward of their shame, and the change is probably an error. Keil and Delitzsch run through the rest of the variants in order, calling the shift from they say to and they say unimportant, but noting that since the divine name Jahve is here for once chosen side by side with Elohim, it had a strong claim to be retained in the last verse; there the fortieth says the Lord thinketh on me, while this turns the hope into a petition, make haste unto me, an innovation in expression caused by taking over the pronoun.

Of the petitions themselves Clarke says most, and says it briefly. Of those who seek his life he asks only that their advance be stopped — they are coming in a body against me, Lord, stop their progress. The cry of Aha, aha he calls a note of supreme contempt. The blessing asked for those who seek God he turns outward: let his glory, mercy and kindness continually appear in the increase of his own work in the souls of his followers.

On the last verse the readings converge on poverty. Clarke renders the words a poor man and a beggar — an afflicted beggar, a sense of whose poverty causes him to beg — and reads the confession that follows as the reason for coming at all: I know thou hast enough, and to spare, and therefore I come to thee. The closing plea he makes as urgent as the opening one, my wants being many, my danger great and my time short, so that the prayer is simply, O God, delay not. Ellicott marks here the sharpest of all the changes from the older psalm, which had said the Lord thinketh on me where this says make haste unto me, O God; Gill notes the same substitution. Keil and Delitzsch let the verse stand as it is written.
